Photograph: Paula Bronstein Since 2025, Paula Bronstein has been photographing wounded Ukrainian servicemen as they learn to live with the loss of sight, hearing and limbs By Luke Harding . Photographs by Paula Bronstein Fri 7 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 02.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google For more than four decades, the US photojournalist Paula Bronstein has travelled to places overlooked by the wider world, including countries scarred by war, such as Afghanistan and Ukraine . Bronstein says her life’s mission has been to “bear witness to critical moments” and to “create images that evoke true empathy in others”. Her prize-winning photographs document political conflict, humanitarian crises and social injustice. Yet she is equally drawn to the quieter moments of everyday life: to “joy and happiness and the full spectrum of human experience”. She attributes her work to an “insatiable curiosity” and a desire to document people’s “enduring humanity” amid tragedy. View image in fullscreen At a workshop in Lviv for blind veterans, Ivan Rozuman receives instruction from a mobility trainer as he learns to navigate the streets. Rozuman joined the military before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. He says he has been wounded twice and undergone more than 50 operations. So much shrapnel remains lodged in his body, he says, that he has lost count. He was first injured during a Kharkiv offensive in 2022 while serving with the 25th Brigade. Ivan lost his sight and has hearing loss. After leaving military service, he was caught in an explosion near his home in in Zaporizhzhia and almost died. Since 2025, Bronstein has been photographing wounded Ukrainian servicemen for a project, Blinded by War. Vladimir Putin’s 2022 invasion has left a generation of young Ukrainian men with life-changing injuries. Most have been hit by kamikaze drones, used extensively by both sides across a sprawling battlefield. View image in fullscreen On 14 February 2023, Vitaliy Veres was injured in Bakhmut. His eyes were damaged, his chin was torn open and both tympanic cavities – the middle ear – were destroyed. He underwent more than 30 surgeries, beginning with military-funded care that left him disillusioned and frustrated. He hopes to popularise adaptive sports for Ukrainian veterans and become a motivational speaker. He is now a bodybuilder and trains in the gym every day. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen ‘Abroad, I’m a hero. At home, people look at me like I’m scary,’ Veres says. He met his partner, Victoria Lysachenko, in their hometown in 2012 and they have a daughter. Her unwavering support has been one of the cornerstones of his recovery. Ukraine is facing the immense challenge of providing medical care, rehabilitation and psychological support to a growing number of wounded military personnel. The country’s healthcare system is struggling to treat the many soldiers who have sustained vision loss. View image in fullscreen Artists at the Imatech medical eye clinic in Kyiv use 3D printers to create realistic eyes. Bronstein’s subjects include Artur Martosich, a competitive weightlifter who runs with a guide, and Serhii Chabanov, a father of three who was blinded and lost an arm in a drone attack near the eastern city of Bakhmut. “I learn something from each new story I do. The people in Ukraine are incredible. What fascinates me is their resilience,” she says. View image in fullscreen Artur Martosich is a war veteran who lost his sight as a result of his injuries. Since then, Martosich has dedicated himself to sport and personal growth. A passionate strongman and powerlifter, he also embraces endurance sports, combining strength training with running and other athletic disciplines, and has won numerous veteran sporting competitions. Martosich was shot in the head from three metres while on a combat mission. He lives with his father and describes sport as the “best form of rehabilitation – physical, spiritual and mental”, adding: “Before the war I used to wrestle. My current goal is to make it into the Ukrainian national team for strongman competitions.” View image in fullscreen Andriy Onopriienko takes dance lessons at a centre for the blind in Kyiv where he can also take part in rock climbing, cooking and learning braille. Another soldier, Andriy Onopriienko, 32, was hit two years ago by tank fire. He lost his eyesight and suffered several facial burns and hearing loss in one ear. “I was in so much pain I begged another comrade to kill me. Now I want to live my life to the fullest, one step at a time and to achieve small things every day,” he says. He lives in the Kyiv family apartment where he grew up. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Recalling the aftermath of his injury, Onopriienko says: ‘I couldn’t see anything, I was worried about my family and had suicidal thoughts as well.’ In July, Bronstein visited the Ukrainian capital’s regional hospital, where she photographed patients undergoing eye surgery. One of them, 30-year-old Rafael Akhmedov, lost his left eye in 2024 when a mortar hit him in the Kharkiv region. He was receiving a scleral implant. Last year, the hospital carried out eye operations on 100 soldiers. View image in fullscreen Mariia Borkhalenko performs surgery on a veteran who lost his eye, inserting a scleral implant “I hope this is my last time here,” Akhemedov says. Asked about his plans for the future, he says: “My wife and I are working on having a kid.” The hospital’s ocular surgeon, Mariia Borkhalenko, says 70% of her patients have lost one or both eyes. “They are victims of FPV drones, bombs, explosions and blast waves.” Many blinded soldiers also lose their hands. “It’s a reflex. When there is a blast people raise their arms,” Borkhalenko says. While some veterans cope well, others become depressed and “asocial”, she adds. “It’s a big number of people, unfortunately. We have psychologists who talk to them and help them to learn to live without hands and sight.” View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Ilya Romantsov, 26, at the Protez Foundation in Kyiv, which provides free prosthetics. Romantsov lost his eyesightand both hands in a first-person view (FPV) Russian drone attack last year. There has been a devastating rise in traumatic hand amputations and loss of vision because FPV drones target individuals directly and detonate at close range. In recent months Russia has stepped up its drone and ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv. Many people shelter in basements and metro stations. Borkhalenko says: “I still get up in the morning and go to work. Doing surgery is my job. Our shared goal is to defeat the enemy and win this war.” Bronstein moves rapidly around the operating theatre, photographing Akhmedov from different angles. She is not squeamish about blood: “I’ve covered conflict for so many years, going back to the horrible bombings in Pakistan, to the war in Afghanistan, and to working in many many hospitals in Kabul. It’s how I want to tell the story.” View image in fullscreen At a Lviv workshop supported by the non-profit Let’s See the Victory , for blind veterans, Yuliya watches as her father, Volodymr, dances with an instructor. She adds: “For me, photography is an intensely personal exploration, seen through my own eyes. I am incredibly fortunate that, at 72, what truly matters is my unwavering passion for my work. I remain deeply curious, always seeking, and profoundly proud to portray what’s possible, even in the darkest corners.” Bronstein’s latest book is called Witnessing Life: A Retrospective . Her pictures have been published and exhibited globally. She spent 15 years as a staff photographer for US newspapers, before working for Getty Images in Asia from 2002 to 2013. Between 2001 and 2021 she covered the war in Afghanistan. Her book Afghanistan: Between Hope and Fear was published in 2016. View image in fullscreen Serhii Chabanov, right, takes part in a weightlifting competition in Brovary for veterans with disabilities. He was severely wounded in a drone attack that caused his to lose him sight and one arm. Chabanov took second place in his category. “My life has unfolded as a continuous conversation with photojournalism. I have given myself entirely to it, and in turn, it has profoundly shaped who I am today,” she says. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgx.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, An emergency response to major wildfires was launched in the Gironde region in late July By James Waterhouse ,Â Paris correspondent Â and Â Marianne Baisnee Published 6 hours ago After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: Why? A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising. But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer. The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors. In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a â¬150,000 (Â£128,000) fine, if convicted. Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Ãtape forest in the Vosges region. "Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est RÃ©publicain, the newspaper that reported the story. Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts. "I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction. The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame. The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues. But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances. "The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying. Devastating European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled Published 29 July 'It's our home, it's our forest': BBC speaks to locals fighting France wildfire Published 29 July Working out how a fire started is, unsurprisingly, not easy. "In periods of drought such as this one, all you need is a simple lighter," explains Eric Dufayet, an officer who investigates fires. Once a fire is out, Eric's first task is to map its outline along the edge of the burnt vegetation, then trace it back to its point of origin. If the wind has been steady, that outline often forms a "V" shape. From there, his team works backwards along the path the flames took. "If someone deliberately starts a fire, they may not have used only one device," he says. It improves the chances of a DNA or fingerprint sample being found. Experts believe arson accounts for only a small fraction of fires. Most are believed to be accidental, with sparks potentially coming from construction work, faulty electrical equipment, cigarette butts and barbecues. "With cigarettes, it's called the '30' rule," says Eric Dufayet. To start a fire, he explains, there must be "a temperature of at least 30C (86F), a maximum of 30% humidity, wind of less than 30km/h (19mph), and at least 30% of the cigarette unburnt." In the current drought, he says it is even easier. If those conditions are met, a fire can easily spread, and fast. Image source, Reuters Image caption, French President Emmanuel Macron called the fires "completely unprecedented" According to Michel Lejoyeux, a professor of psychiatry and addictive behaviour at Paris 7 University, people who start fires fall into three categories: those who are careless, those who benefit - with an insurance payout, for example - and pyromaniacs. "The pyromaniac doesn't get money, has no spirit of revenge, has no utility of the fire, but he likes the fire," he says. However, pyromania is a rare psychiatric disorder that Lejoyeux says is very difficult to diagnose, and accounts for few arson convictions. Lawyer Muriel Gestas, who has handled several such cases, says some firefighters alleged to have started fires may have wanted to be seen as saviours. For others - notably volunteers earning tax-free overtime - the motive may be financial. Amid concerns over how officials are pursuing suspects, broader worries about wildfires are far from abating. Forecasts suggest France's next heatwave is only days away. President Emmanuel Macron says criticism should not be the priority right now. "We will have to replant and rebuild a different kind of forest because we must adapt to the structural conditions of climate change," he said this week. "The time for reviewing lessons learned will come," he insisted. "In the meantime, the country must remain united." Even so, the damage these fires have inflicted on the environment, hundreds of homes, tourism, local businesses and air quality has left the French public with a lot of questions. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: 1:14 Russian drone hits academy of sciences in Kyiv, killing one – video Ukraine Daytime Russian strike on Kyiv’s science academy kills at least one Three others wounded as jet-powered drones increasingly target Ukraine’s capital, with medical centre also hit Pjotr Sauer in Kyiv Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.16 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Russian drone hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv on Monday, killing at least one person, in the latest daytime attack on Ukraine’s capital. Flames tore through the historic building as people clambered out of first- and second-floor windows to escape, in dramatic scenes increasingly familiar in the heavily bombarded city. At least one person was killed and three others were wounded, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, who said the injured had been taken to hospital. The 19th-century building stands close to the German embassy, the National Opera, St Volodymyr’s Cathedral and several government buildings. Anatoliy Zagorodny, the president of the national academy, said the blast struck while many staff members were inside. Standing outside the burning building, he said he did not know why Russia had targeted a leading centre of scientific research. “We are not connected with the military. This is an attack on science. It is terrorism,” he said. He feared some of his colleagues could still be trapped inside the academy. While the sciences building is a civilian scientific institution, it has longstanding ties to Ukraine’s defence sector. Among those injured in Monday’s strike was Volodymyr Horbulin, the academy’s first vice-president and a former high-ranking security official. Another Russian drone struck a nearby private medical centre, killing at least one person. View image in fullscreen The building of a private medical clinic was also hit by a Russian drone in Kyiv. Photograph: Nikoletta Stoyanova/Getty Images Russian strikes over the past week involving missiles and increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones have hit apartment blocks, offices, warehouses and datacentres across the capital, killing and wounding civilians almost daily and giving Kyiv an increasingly frontline feel as it faces some of its most sustained bombardment since the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. The drone and missile campaign is designed to grind down public resilience and damage the economy. Monday’s double strike is likely to raise fresh concerns over Ukraine’s ability to protect even the most heavily guarded parts of the capital. The newer jet-powered drones fly faster and are harder to intercept than the older Shahed or Geran-2 models that were the backbone of Moscow’s air campaign. Ukraine is racing to develop and manufacture interceptors capable of bringing them down. Graphic showing the increasing speed of Russian drones and missiles Moscow has also changed its tactics, launching more attacks in daylight hours so that residents in major cities have to spend more of the day under air raid alerts. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Buildings hit during daytime strikes are often occupied because many Ukrainians work through drone alerts rather than spend hours in shelters. The long-range drone war: Ukraine and Russia scramble for supremacy in the skies Read more Meanwhile, a Russian jet-powered drone struck western Ukraine near the border crossing with Poland, prompting Warsaw to issue an alert warning of a possible air attack and urging residents in the eastern Lublin region to seek shelter. Russian forces have increasingly targeted Ukrainian border crossings with Poland and Moldova, leading Kyiv to consider relocating joint customs checkpoints to the territory of neighbouring countries. “It’s again a threat very close to our border,” said Lt Col Jacek Goryszewski, speaking to Poland’s broadcaster TVN24. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, called on western countries to intensify their pressure on Russia. “Every Russian terrorist attack is a loss of life that could have been prevented if pressure on Russia had finally become total,” he wrote on X on Monday. “The world must understand that terrorists will go further if they are not stopped here, in Ukraine. And we cannot turn a blind eye to such brutal strikes.” Russia has signalled that its attacks on Ukraine could intensify, and US-brokered efforts to end the war show little sign of progress. “Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters on Monday, referring to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russian territory. “That is happening right now.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky EU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato Ukraine targets Moscow with hundreds of drones on final day of Russian election Latvia’s president warns that Europe is not up to date with drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine Russian strike on passenger train will not deter Ukraine’s backers, Nato chief says Trains carrying Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief may have been targeted in Russian strike, officials say Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call.’ Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPA View image in fullscreen ‘Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call.’ Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPA Opinion Europe The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump Editorial If ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harm Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.25 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.27 EDT Share F ollowing the Brexit referendum in 2016, Marine Le Pen was in a predictably celebratory mood. Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, she told one interviewer, was the first breach in the “Brussels Wall”. Ms Le Pen’s Front National party was at that point committed to taking France down the same path, given the chance. But as the UK’s self-inflicted economic wounds became a cautionary tale for the rest of Europe, the notion of Frexit was put on ice. Instead, Ms Le Pen now hopes to lead far-right allies in hollowing out the EU from within. This month, both she and the leader of Alternative für Deutschland, Alice Weidel, outlined their visions of a “Europe of nations” in which EU institutions would be stripped of both cash and power. Ms Weidel’s “new deal for Europe” would abolish elections to the European parliament, and seek German opt-outs in areas such as migration, defence and common borrowing. Ms Le Pen’s party, now called National Rally, proposes slashing French contributions to the EU budget by 60% over a five-year presidential term, and ending the role of Brussels in proposing common policies for the 27 member states. View image in fullscreen Alice Weidel. Photograph: AFP/Getty Similar ideas have long circulated in far-right thinktanks. But they are now in the programmes of parties that lead the polls in France and Germany – Europe’s historic engines of integration. Ms Weidel has targeted 2029, when the next German election is due to take place, as the year in which a critical mass of anti-EU leaders can begin to effectively unravel the European project. By then, Eurosceptic ultra-nationalist parties could conceivably be in power in France, Italy and Poland. Faced with plotting in plain sight and a putative timetable for action, the response of pro-European forces has been distinctly underwhelming. From the economy to the climate emergency and security, Europe faces challenges that can only be properly addressed through the greater pooling of resources, allowing it to punch its continental weight. Mario Draghi, the former head of the European Central Bank, has warned that without an industrial policy to compete with China and the US, the continent faces an existential struggle. But other than the beleaguered and soon-to-be-departed French president Emmanuel Macron, it has been hard to find any EU leader speaking with the same sense of urgency. Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call. The kind of Europe they envisage would be less than the sum of its parts, distracted and weakened by competing national interests. In relation to defence, the moves towards European strategic autonomy would be undermined. The green transition, in the absence of collectively agreed goals, would stall. Adopting such a direction of travel would be an act of continental self-harm, opening up vulnerabilities that Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin (and any Maga successor to Donald Trump) would eagerly exploit. As a pivotal period in the history of the EU approaches, the time to start making such counter-arguments is now. The case for a strong Europe at a time of geopolitical volatility and anxiety is overwhelming. But it will need vigorous advocates as a battle for hearts and minds looms. For the time being, to paraphrase WB Yeats , the pro-Europeans appear to lack all conviction, while their opponents are full of passionate intensity.
